tierWindow.goal: Understand academic writing as a process you work through, and be able to get a draft down and get the basics right.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Recognition, recall, description and guided application (understand and identify).
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Well-defined, one idea at a time; settled distinctions such as editing versus proofreading.
tierWindow.autonomy: High scaffolding; worked examples; feedback confirms and explains; frequent low-stakes checks.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No prior experience of treating academic writing as a staged process is assumed. The learner is early in their studies and has written essays at school but tends to see writing as a single sitting that must come out right first time; teach the process and the basics from first principles.

subThemes.label: Academic writing as a process of distinct stages, not a single act of getting it right first time
Three common (false) assumptions students make about academic writing
The writing cycle: the stages a piece of writing moves through, with planning at its heart
Understanding the task: the steer and the keywords of a question
Planning before drafting, and getting a first draft down rather than waiting for the perfect version
The four pillars of effective writing that recur across genres
Getting the basics right: structure and organisation, and clarity and precision (the SVO sentence)
Editing versus proofreading, and the common errors in student writing

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, writing as a process: why a good piece of work is made in stages, not in one sitting. Second, understanding the task and getting a draft down: reading the question, planning, and getting started. Third, getting the basics right: editing a draft for structure and clarity. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about academic writing: not a single talent some people have and others do not, but a process you can learn to work through. By the end you will be able to describe writing as a series of stages, plan a piece and get a first draft down, and improve that draft by getting the basics of structure and clarity right.

These are not abstract study skills. Writing is how most of your work is assessed, in every subject. Knowing the process, and having a few reliable habits, changes how you start, how you revise, and the marks your work earns.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: describe writing as a process, plan and draft, improve a draft by getting the basics right.

practiceConnection.academic: Academic writing is the main way your learning is judged. Every essay, report and reflective piece you are set draws on the same underlying process: understand the task, plan, draft, and revise. Build the habit now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the clear, organised writing that professional work later asks of you.

grounding.note: states/rates/tests the three course outcomes (AL-4/AL-5/AL-6)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced academic writing courses take the process into building an argument, using sources, and writing within your own discipline. Going wider: the same habits underpin Criticality, Referencing and Researching, where you put clear writing to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Academic writing is no longer a single daunting act: it is a process you can work through. You can describe its stages, that is, understanding the task, planning, drafting and revising. You can read a task for its steer and keywords, plan, and get a first draft down rather than waiting for perfect sentences. And you can improve that draft by getting the basics right: a clear structure and clear sentences, editing before you proofread. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, this process is something you use in every module. Each essay you plan before you write, each rough draft you get down and then improve, each piece you edit for structure before proofreading, is the same process at work. It is also what professional life rewards: clear, organised writing produced to a deadline travels well beyond your degree.
